Varves are light-and-dark pairs of lake layers, one pair per year, counted like tree rings
Turbidity currents (underwater avalanches) leave graded beds called turbidites; one off Newfoundland in 1929 snapped undersea cables
Uluru is arkose, a feldspar-rich kind; Kata Tjuta is conglomerate; Zion’s cliffs show cross-beds of ancient sand dunes
Jordan’s Petra was carved into cliffs of one kind of them (sandstone), which also forms the more than 2,000 natural arches of Utah’s Arches National Park
Chert and flint are very hard kinds made of microscopic quartz crystals; early humans chipped them into tools
Salt and gypsum beds under the Mediterranean show it nearly dried up about 6 million years ago (the Messinian salinity crisis)
NASA’s Curiosity rover (2012) found conglomerate and lake-bottom mudstone in Mars’s Gale Crater

trap.title: The class, not one rock
trap.body: Tossups on sedimentary rocks are packed with examples like sandstone, shale, limestone, and coal, and with words like “fossils” and “strata,” which tempts players to buzz with one of them. The question wants the whole class of rocks. Igneous rocks (cooled from melted rock) and metamorphic rocks (changed by heat and pressure) are the other two classes, and they are wrong here.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this class of rocks” or “these rocks” means the category. Layers, cementing, sediment, fossils, and Steno’s law of superposition mean sedimentary; cooling magma or lava means igneous; heat and pressure without melting means metamorphic. Saying just “sediment” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Sedimentary rocks (prompt on clastic rocks or sediment; do not accept “igneous rocks,” “metamorphic rocks,” or a single rock like “shale”)

topics.name: Shale
topics.kicker: Fine-grained rock of hardened mud · Splits into thin, flat layers
topics.briefing: Shale is a soft, fine-grained rock made of mud: tiny flakes of clay and grains of silt that settled in quiet water and were pressed into thin layers. It is the most common sedimentary rock, and it splits easily into sheets. Dark shales rich in ancient plankton are the source of much of the world’s oil and natural gas, and Canada’s Burgess Shale preserves some of the most famous fossils on Earth.
topics.answerHtml: Shale (accept oil shale or black shale; prompt on mudstone, mudrock, or sedimentary rock; do not accept “slate,” “schist,” or “shale gas”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1909, Charles Walcott discovered a layer of this rock high in British Columbia’s Yoho National Park that preserves soft-bodied Cambrian animals like five-eyed Opabinia. Stephen Jay Gould’s book _Wonderful Life_ describes the strange creatures from that layer, which is named for nearby Mount Burgess.
tossups.r: This rock splits easily into thin sheets. For 10 points, name this common sedimentary rock made of hardened mud.

tossups.p: Fossils from this rock near Holzmaden, Germany, show that Jurassic ichthyosaurs gave birth to live young, and some even preserve the outline of their skin. Germany’s Messel Pit, an old quarry of an oil-rich kind of this rock, holds fossils of tiny early horses from about 47 million years ago.
tossups.r: Heat and pressure turn this rock into slate. For 10 points, name this fine-grained sedimentary rock that splits into thin layers.

tossups.p: The Green River Formation of Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming holds the world’s largest known deposits of the oil-rich kind of this rock, along with huge numbers of fossil fish such as Knightia, Wyoming’s state fossil. Heating that kind of this rock releases oil from a solid organic material called kerogen.
tossups.r: This rock forms from mud that settles in quiet water. For 10 points, name this most common sedimentary rock.

tossups.p: In the late 1990s, George Mitchell’s company found a cheaper way to crack Texas’s Barnett formation of this rock with high-pressure water, sand, and chemicals, starting a drilling boom. Combining that method with horizontal drilling later opened up Pennsylvania’s Marcellus formation of this rock.
tossups.r: That process, hydraulic fracturing, is nicknamed fracking. For 10 points, name this fine-grained sedimentary rock that holds trapped natural gas.

tossups.p: China’s Chengjiang [“chung-jyahng”] fossils, found in layers of this rock in Yunnan Province, preserve soft-bodied animals about 10 million years older than Canada’s Burgess fossils. Mud buried those animals so quickly that even their soft parts were preserved.
tossups.r: This rock forms from compacted clay and silt. For 10 points, name this rock that splits into thin layers and turns into slate under heat and pressure.

tossups.p: Geologists call this rock’s habit of splitting along thin, parallel layers fissility, and that property separates it from mudstone, a similar rock that breaks into blocky chunks. Its grains, mostly flakes of clay minerals with some silt, are too small to see with the naked eye.
tossups.r: It is the most common sedimentary rock on Earth. For 10 points, name this rock made of compacted mud.

tossups.p: With rising heat and pressure, this rock changes into a series of metamorphic rocks: after the first one come phyllite [“FILL-ite”], then schist [“SHIST”], and finally gneiss [“NICE”]. In the first rock of that series, a new direction of splitting called cleavage often cuts across this rock’s original layers.
tossups.r: That first metamorphic rock is slate, once used for roofs and chalkboards. For 10 points, name this sedimentary rock made of hardened mud, which splits into thin layers.

tossups.p: This rock is black when it holds lots of carbon from ancient plankton and plants, and red or purple when it holds rusty iron minerals like hematite. Its dark, carbon-rich kinds are the source rocks for much of the world’s oil and natural gas.
tossups.r: It forms from mud that settles slowly in calm water, such as lake bottoms and deep seafloors. For 10 points, name this fine-grained sedimentary rock.

tossups.p: Because oil and water cannot easily flow through its tightly packed clay flakes, this rock often acts as a seal, or cap rock, that traps oil and natural gas in more porous sandstone beneath it. Weathering breaks this rock down into clay-rich soil.
tossups.r: Heat and pressure turn this rock into slate. For 10 points, name this common sedimentary rock made of compacted mud.

tossups.p: Marrella, a small arthropod with long sweeping spines, is the most common animal in a famous fossil bed made of this rock, where underwater mudflows buried creatures so quickly that even their soft parts were preserved. The early chordate Pikaia also comes from that fossil bed in the Canadian Rockies.
tossups.r: That fossil bed is named for Mount Burgess. For 10 points, name this dark, fine-grained rock that splits into thin layers.

tossups.p: This rock belongs to the mudrocks, whose grains are finer than about one-sixteenth of a millimeter, the boundary between silt and sand on the Wentworth scale. Its tiny clay flakes settle only in quiet water, so it often forms on deep seafloors, lake bottoms, and river floodplains.
tossups.r: Sandstone forms from coarser grains, but this rock forms from mud. For 10 points, name this rock that splits easily into thin layers.

tossups.p: In the Grand Canyon, the soft, greenish Bright Angel layer of this rock holds Cambrian trilobite fossils and burrows. Because this rock crumbles more easily than the sandstone and limestone around it, its layers wear back into gentle slopes between steep cliffs.
tossups.r: Its grains are tiny flakes of clay pressed together. For 10 points, name this most common sedimentary rock.

tossups.p: North Dakota’s Bakken formation, which includes two dark layers of this rock, became one of the biggest oil-producing areas in the United States during the 2010s. Supporters of drilling in this rock point to cheaper energy and jobs, while critics worry about water supplies and earthquakes linked to disposing of wastewater underground.
tossups.r: Hydraulic fracturing, or fracking, cracks this rock to free trapped oil and natural gas. For 10 points, name this fine-grained sedimentary rock.

tossups.p: Colorado’s Florissant Fossil Beds preserve delicate insects, spiders, and leaves in paper-thin layers of this rock that formed in an ancient lake about 34 million years ago. Estonia burned an oil-rich kind of this rock for decades to make most of its electricity.
tossups.r: This rock splits easily into thin sheets, a property called fissility. For 10 points, name this most common sedimentary rock.

tossups.p: Clay minerals such as illite [“ILL-ite”] and kaolinite [“KAY-uh-lih-nite”] make up much of this rock, along with tiny grains of quartz. Ground up and mixed with limestone, this rock helps make Portland cement, and it is also fired to make bricks.
tossups.r: This rock forms from hardened mud and splits into thin layers. For 10 points, name this most common sedimentary rock.

Colorado’s Florissant Fossil Beds keep insects in paper-thin layers of it; Estonia burned an oil-rich kind for most of its electricity
The Grand Canyon’s greenish Bright Angel layer of it holds Cambrian trilobites and wears back into gentle slopes
Its clay minerals include illite and kaolinite, mixed with tiny quartz grains

trap.title: Shale, slate, or schist?
trap.body: Shale’s stock clue is that heat and pressure turn it into slate, so players who hear “slate” or “thin sheets” sometimes answer with the metamorphic rock instead. Slate, phyllite, schist, and gneiss are all different answer lines. Saying only “sedimentary rock” or “mudstone” earns a prompt, because the question wants this one rock.
trap.fix: Mud, clay, fissility, fracking for natural gas, black source rocks, and the Burgess fossils mean shale. Metamorphism, roofing tiles, chalkboards, and slaty cleavage mean slate. If you are prompted, say “shale.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Shale (accept oil shale; prompt on mudstone or sedimentary rock; do not accept “slate”)

topics.name: Caves
topics.kicker: Natural underground hollows · Most form as acidic water dissolves limestone
topics.dates: Dissolved out of rock over many thousands of years
topics.briefing: Most caves form when rainwater, made slightly acidic by carbon dioxide, seeps into cracks in limestone and slowly dissolves the rock away. Inside, dripping water leaves behind stony icicles: stalactites hang from the ceiling and stalagmites rise from the floor. Kentucky’s Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system on Earth, and France’s Lascaux Cave holds paintings of animals made about 17,000 years ago.
topics.answerHtml: Caves (accept cave, caverns, or grottoes; accept kinds like limestone caves or sea caves; prompt on holes or chambers; do not accept “karst,” “sinkholes,” “stalactites,” or a single named cave)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1889, the Frenchman Édouard-Alfred Martel explored the underground river of the Gouffre de Padirac [“GOO-fruh duh pah-dee-RAHK”], and in 1895 he founded a French scientific society devoted to exploring these features. Mineral deposits that grow inside them are called speleothems, from Greek words for one of these features and for a deposit.
tossups.r: The scientific study of these features is called speleology. For 10 points, name these natural underground openings, where stalactites grow.

tossups.p: In the late 1830s, an enslaved guide named Stephen Bishop began exploring and mapping miles of one of these features in Kentucky, where miners had dug saltpeter for gunpowder during the War of 1812. In 1972, explorers linked that system to the nearby Flint Ridge system, making the combined network the longest known example on Earth.
tossups.r: That system is Kentucky’s Mammoth one. For 10 points, name these underground openings, where stalactites hang from the ceiling.

tossups.p: A cowboy named Jim White began exploring one of these features near Carlsbad, New Mexico, around 1898, after seeing a huge cloud of bats rising from the ground. Unlike most of these features, that one and nearby Lechuguilla [“leh-chuh-GEE-yuh”] were dissolved mostly by sulfuric acid formed from gases rising out of oil deposits.
tossups.r: Its Big Room is a vast chamber decorated with stalactites and stalagmites. For 10 points, name these underground openings, whose study is called speleology.

tossups.p: In 1940, four teenagers in southwestern France found one of these features at Lascaux [“lass-KOH”], whose walls are covered with paintings of horses, bulls, and deer made about 17,000 years ago. It was closed to visitors in 1963 because their breath was damaging the paintings, and copies were built nearby.
tossups.r: Prehistoric people painted on the walls of many of these features. For 10 points, name these natural underground chambers.

tossups.p: In 1879, a young girl named María Sanz de Sautuola looked up and spotted paintings of bison on the ceiling of Altamira, one of these features in northern Spain. Many experts at first refused to believe that Stone Age people could have made such skillful art.
tossups.r: Stalactites hang from the ceilings of these features. For 10 points, name these natural underground openings.

tossups.p: Werner Herzog filmed a 3D documentary inside Chauvet [“shoh-VAY”], one of these features in southern France whose charcoal drawings of lions, rhinoceroses, and horses are more than 30,000 years old. Jean-Marie Chauvet and two fellow explorers discovered it in 1994.
tossups.r: Many of these features form when water dissolves limestone. For 10 points, name these underground openings, home to stalactites and stalagmites.

tossups.p: A local man named Ho Khanh found the entrance to Vietnam’s Son Doong, and British explorers who mapped it in 2009 showed that it has the largest known passage of any of these features. Parts of its roof have collapsed, letting in enough sunlight for a jungle to grow inside.
tossups.r: Explorers of these features are sometimes called spelunkers. For 10 points, name these natural underground hollows, often dissolved out of limestone.

tossups.p: In 2000, miners in Mexico’s Naica [“nah-EE-kah”] mine broke into one of these features filled with gypsum crystals up to about 12 meters long, so hot and humid that explorers needed cooling suits. The crystals had grown slowly in hot, mineral-rich water that once filled the chamber.
tossups.r: Limestone examples of these features are often decorated with stalactites. For 10 points, name these natural underground openings.

tossups.p: The olm, a pale, nearly blind salamander from Slovenia, is a troglobite, an animal that can survive only in these dark places. Eyeless forms of the Mexican tetra fish, which lost their eyes over many generations, also live only in these places.
tossups.r: Bats often roost in these features, where stalactites hang from the ceiling. For 10 points, name these natural underground hollows.

tossups.p: In 1938, Nathaniel Kleitman and a colleague spent 32 days deep inside one of these features in Kentucky, trying to live on a 28-hour day. Blind fish and white, eyeless shrimp in that system have adapted to its total darkness.
tossups.r: That system, Kentucky’s Mammoth one, is the longest known on Earth. For 10 points, name these underground openings, often carved out of limestone.

tossups.p: Thin, hollow tubes called soda straws are young versions of a formation that hangs in these places, while twisting helictites [“HEL-ik-tites”] seem to grow sideways or even upward against gravity. Sheets of calcite called flowstone coat their walls and floors.
tossups.r: Stalactites hang from their ceilings, while stalagmites rise from their floors. For 10 points, name these natural underground openings.

tossups.p: Visitors to Waitomo [“wy-TOH-moh”] in New Zealand ride boats through one of these features lit by thousands of glowworms, the glowing larvae of a kind of fly. On the Scottish island of Staffa, Fingal’s, a sea-carved example lined with basalt columns, inspired Felix Mendelssohn’s overture _The Hebrides_.
tossups.r: Most of these features form when rainwater dissolves limestone. For 10 points, name these underground hollows, studied in speleology.

tossups.p: In 2018, international divers rescued twelve boys from a youth soccer team and their coach after monsoon floodwaters trapped them for more than two weeks inside Tham Luang, one of these features in northern Thailand. A former Thai Navy SEAL diver died during the rescue.
tossups.r: Stalactites and stalagmites form inside many of these features. For 10 points, name these natural underground openings, explored by spelunkers.

tossups.p: Scientists date the growth layers of speleothems from these places using uranium and thorium, and the mix of oxygen atoms in those layers records rainfall from thousands of years ago. Those formations grow when dripping water loses carbon dioxide and leaves calcium carbonate behind.
tossups.r: Formations that hang from the ceilings of these places are called stalactites. For 10 points, name these natural underground openings.

tossups.p: In 2010, scientists identified the Denisovans, close relatives of Neanderthals, from DNA in a finger bone found in one of these features in Siberia. Lava tubes are hollow examples of these features that form when the outside of a lava flow hardens while molten rock drains out from inside.
tossups.r: Most of these features form when carbonic acid in groundwater dissolves limestone. For 10 points, name these natural underground openings.

trap.title: Not stalactites, not karst
trap.body: Tossups on caves are full of stalactites, stalagmites, sinkholes, and limestone, so players blurt out one of those words instead of the feature itself. Those are separate answers here. Famous examples like Mammoth Cave or Lascaux are wrong too, because the question wants the general feature.
trap.fix: Wait for “name these underground openings” and answer caves (caverns is fine too). Stalactites hang from the ceiling and stalagmites rise from the floor, and karst is the whole landscape of dissolved limestone, including sinkholes and springs.
trap.line: Real answer line: Caves (accept caverns; do not accept “stalactites,” “stalagmites,” or “karst”)

topics.name: Mesozoic Era
topics.kicker: The “Age of Reptiles,” about 252 to 66 million years ago · Home of the dinosaurs
topics.briefing: The Mesozoic Era, from about 252 to 66 million years ago, is nicknamed the “Age of Reptiles”: dinosaurs ruled the land, pterosaurs flew overhead, and giant marine reptiles swam the seas. It is split into three periods, the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous. It began right after the largest mass extinction in Earth’s history and ended when an asteroid struck Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, wiping out every dinosaur except the birds.
topics.answerHtml: Mesozoic Era (prompt on Age of Reptiles or Age of Dinosaurs; do not accept “Triassic,” “Jurassic,” “Cretaceous,” “Paleozoic,” or “Cenozoic”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The English geologist John Phillips named this era in 1840 from Greek words meaning “middle life,” placing it between an era of “ancient life” and one of “new life.” Ammonites, coiled relatives of squid, are used as index fossils to split its rock layers into zones.
tossups.r: Its three periods are the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous. For 10 points, name this era, nicknamed the “Age of Reptiles.”

tossups.p: Lystrosaurus [“liss-troh-SOR-us”], a stocky, tusked plant-eater, survived the mass extinction that began this era and became one of the most common land animals of its first period. Fossils of Lystrosaurus found in Antarctica, India, and South Africa show that those lands were once joined in the supercontinent Pangaea.
tossups.r: This era ended when an asteroid struck Mexico 66 million years ago. For 10 points, name this era, the “Age of Reptiles.”

tossups.p: In 1977, Geerat Vermeij named a “marine revolution” for this era, after noticing that shell-crushing predators spread during it while snails evolved thicker, spinier shells and clams burrowed deeper. Mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and ichthyosaurs were giant reptiles that swam in its seas.
tossups.r: Dinosaurs ruled the land during this era. For 10 points, name this era that includes the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods.

tossups.p: In 1923, Roy Chapman Andrews’s team found nests of fossil eggs from this era in Mongolia’s Gobi, at a site called the Flaming Cliffs. Scientists later showed that many of those eggs had been laid by Oviraptor, whose name means “egg thief,” and its close relatives, rather than by Protoceratops.
tossups.r: Non-bird dinosaurs died out at the end of this era. For 10 points, name this era, the “Age of Reptiles,” which followed the Paleozoic.

tossups.p: In 1834, Friedrich von Alberti named the first period of this era for a set of three rock layers in Germany. Hundreds of skeletons of Coelophysis [“see-loh-FY-sis”], a slender, early meat-eater, were found together at Ghost Ranch in New Mexico, in rocks from that first period.
tossups.r: That first period, the Triassic, was followed by the Jurassic and Cretaceous. For 10 points, name this era, the “Age of Reptiles.”

tossups.p: In 1822, the Belgian geologist Jean d’Omalius d’Halloy named the last period of this era after the Latin word for chalk. Late in that period, a shallow sea called the Western Interior Seaway split North America into eastern and western landmasses.
tossups.r: That last period, the Cretaceous, ended with the extinction of the non-bird dinosaurs. For 10 points, name this era, which came between the Paleozoic and the Cenozoic.

tossups.p: In 1980, Luis and Walter Alvarez argued that a thin clay layer rich in iridium, found where rocks from the end of this era meet younger rocks around the world, was left by a huge impact from space. Grains of shocked quartz in that layer also point to an impact.
tossups.r: The crater, Chicxulub [“CHEEK-shoo-loob”], lies beneath Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, and the impact wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs. For 10 points, name this era that began about 252 million years ago.

tossups.p: This era began right after the largest mass extinction in Earth’s history, nicknamed the “Great Dying,” which wiped out most species in the oceans. Scientists link that disaster to enormous volcanic eruptions in what is now Russia that built the Siberian Traps.
tossups.r: This era ended 66 million years ago with the extinction of the non-bird dinosaurs. For 10 points, name this era, often called the “Age of Reptiles.”

tossups.p: A fossil of Repenomamus, a meat-eating mammal from this era found in China, had the bones of a young Psittacosaurus [“sih-TAK-uh-SOR-us”] in its stomach. Most mammals of this era, though, were small, and many probably came out mainly at night. The earliest mammals appeared during this era’s first period.
tossups.r: Dinosaurs dominated the land during this era. For 10 points, name this era of the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods.

tossups.p: Gideon Mantell named Iguanodon in 1825 because its fossil teeth, found in English rocks from this era, looked like a giant iguana’s. In 1854, Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins built life-size models of Iguanodon and other animals from this era for a London park.
tossups.r: In 1842, Richard Owen named the dinosaurs, which ruled the land during this era. For 10 points, name this era, the “Age of Reptiles.”

tossups.p: Quetzalcoatlus [“ket-sul-koh-AT-lus”], a pterosaur from late in this era found in Texas, had a wingspan of about 10 meters and is one of the largest flying animals ever known. Pterosaurs first took to the air during this era’s first period and died out at its end.
tossups.r: Dinosaurs ruled the land below them. For 10 points, name this era, which included the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods.

tossups.p: In 1996, scientists described Sinosauropteryx [“SY-noh-sor-OP-ter-iks”], a small meat-eater from China’s Liaoning Province that was covered in simple, fuzzy feathers. Fossils like it support the idea that birds evolved during this era from small, two-legged meat-eaters called theropods.
tossups.r: Archaeopteryx, an early bird, lived in the middle of this era. For 10 points, name this era, home to the dinosaurs.

tossups.p: Charles Darwin called the sudden spread of flowering plants late in this era an “abominable mystery.” Before then, forests in this era were dominated by conifers, cycads, and ginkgoes, and grasses were rare or absent for most of it.
tossups.r: Dinosaurs fed on those plants during this era. For 10 points, name this era, which spanned the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods.

tossups.p: For most of this era, Earth had a warm greenhouse climate with no large ice sheets at the poles, and sea levels late in this era were far higher than modern ones. The supercontinent Pangaea broke apart during this era, opening the Atlantic Ocean.
tossups.r: This era came between the Paleozoic and the Cenozoic. For 10 points, name this era, the “Age of Reptiles.”

tossups.p: Mary Anning dug ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons from this era out of the seaside cliffs at Lyme Regis, England, in the early 1800s, and her finds helped show that whole groups of animals could go extinct. Huge marine lizards called mosasaurs ruled the seas near this era’s end.
tossups.r: Dinosaurs ruled the land during this era, which ended 66 million years ago. For 10 points, name this era that includes the Jurassic period.

trap.title: The era, not a period
trap.body: Mesozoic tossups are packed with clues about the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous, so players often name one of those periods instead of the whole era. Those are separate answer lines, and so are the Paleozoic (before it) and the Cenozoic (after it). Nicknames like “Age of Reptiles” earn only a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for “this era”: clues that span the first dinosaurs, the Great Dying, and the asteroid impact mean the Mesozoic Era. If you hear “this period” with Stegosaurus or Archaeopteryx, it is the Jurassic; Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops, and the asteroid point to the Cretaceous.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mesozoic Era (prompt on Age of Reptiles; do not accept “Triassic,” “Jurassic,” or “Cretaceous”)

topics.name: Deserts
topics.kicker: Places that get very little rain · Cover about a third of Earth’s land
topics.dates: Get less than about 25 cm (10 in) of precipitation a year
topics.briefing: A desert is any place that gets very little precipitation, usually less than about 25 centimeters (10 inches) a year, so it can be scorching like the Sahara or freezing like Antarctica, the largest desert of all. Cacti store water in their thick stems, camels can go days without drinking, and winds pile sand into towering dunes. In Chile’s Atacama, some weather stations have never recorded rain.
topics.answerHtml: Deserts (accept desert biome; accept hot, cold, or polar deserts; prompt on arid lands; do not accept “Sahara,” another single desert, “dunes,” or “tundra”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the Köppen climate system, these places get the code BW, from the German word Wüste [“VOO-stuh”], with an h added for hot ones and a k, for kalt, for cold ones. Steppes, which get a bit more rain, are labeled BS instead.
tossups.r: These places are often defined as getting less than about 25 centimeters of precipitation a year. For 10 points, name these very dry regions, like the Sahara.

tossups.p: Fog-basking beetles in the Namib [“NAH-mib”] tilt their bodies into the morning fog so that droplets roll down their backs into their mouths. The Namib, along Africa’s southwest coast, is often called the oldest of these places, and it is home to _Welwitschia_ [“wel-WITCH-ee-uh”], a plant that grows only two leaves in its whole life.
tossups.r: Cold ocean currents help create these dry places along some coasts. For 10 points, name these regions that get very little rain.

tossups.p: Astronomers built the ALMA radio telescope array high in Chile’s Atacama because the air there is so dry, and NASA has tested Mars rovers in its barren soil. Some weather stations in the Atacama have never recorded rain, making it the driest of these places outside the poles.
tossups.r: The largest of these places is Antarctica, and the largest hot one is the Sahara. For 10 points, name these very dry regions.

tossups.p: A thin, dark coating of manganese and iron oxides called rock varnish builds up on stones in these places over thousands of years, and ancient people scratched pictures called petroglyphs into it. Winds sandblast some rocks in these places into faceted shapes called ventifacts.
tossups.r: Sand dunes cover parts of these places, though many are mostly rock and gravel. For 10 points, name these dry regions, like the Mojave and the Sahara.

tossups.p: The highest air temperature ever officially recorded, 134 degrees Fahrenheit, was measured in 1913 at Furnace Creek in Death Valley, part of the Mojave, one of these places. Death Valley’s Badwater Basin is the lowest point in North America.
tossups.r: Saguaro cacti grow in the nearby Sonoran, another of these places. For 10 points, name these dry regions that get very little rain.

tossups.p: Prehistoric rock paintings of swimmers in southwestern Egypt and of cattle herds in Algeria’s Tassili n’Ajjer show that the region around them was green and wet until about 5,000 years ago. Dust from that region blows across the Atlantic and helps fertilize the Amazon rainforest.
tossups.r: That region, the Sahara, is the largest hot one of these places. For 10 points, name these regions that get very little rain.

tossups.p: The Rub’ al Khali, or “Empty Quarter,” of the Arabian Peninsula is the largest unbroken sand sea, or erg, of any of these places. Crescent-shaped barchan [“bar-KAHN”] dunes point their horns downwind, while star dunes form where winds blow from many directions.
tossups.r: Cacti and camels are adapted to life in these places. For 10 points, name these dry regions, like the Sahara and the Gobi.

tossups.p: Kangaroo rats in these places can survive without ever drinking, getting the water they need from the seeds they eat, and fennec foxes shed body heat through their enormous ears. Many animals in these places hunt at night to avoid the heat.
tossups.r: Camels, which store fat in their humps, can go days without water in these places. For 10 points, name these very dry regions.

tossups.p: Moist air drops its rain as it rises over a mountain range, so the far side, in the rain shadow, often becomes one of these places, like the Great Basin behind California’s Sierra Nevada. Others form near 30 degrees latitude, where dry air sinks in giant loops called Hadley cells.
tossups.r: The Sahara is the largest hot one of these places. For 10 points, name these regions that get very little precipitation.

tossups.p: In 1935, the pilot Antoine de Saint-Exupéry crashed in one of these places in Egypt and nearly died of thirst before a Bedouin rescued him. That crash inspired the narrator of his book _The Little Prince_, a pilot whose plane breaks down in one of these places.
tossups.r: Frank Herbert’s novel _Dune_ is set on a planet that is almost entirely one of these places. For 10 points, name these dry regions, including the Sahara.

tossups.p: Australia’s thorny devil lizard survives in these places by letting water creep along tiny grooves between its scales to the corners of its mouth. The Gila [“HEE-luh”] monster, a venomous lizard of these places in the American Southwest, stores fat in its thick tail.
tossups.r: Cacti and other succulents store water in their thick stems in these places. For 10 points, name these very dry regions.

tossups.p: The McMurdo Dry Valleys near the Ross Sea, where fierce winds sweep away snow and almost none falls, are so dry that NASA studies them as a model for Mars. Polar examples of these places also cover much of the Arctic.
tossups.r: Because it gets so little precipitation, Antarctica is the largest of these places. For 10 points, name these dry regions, whose largest hot example is the Sahara.

tossups.p: The Gobi of Mongolia and China, a cold example of these places, lies in the rain shadow of the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau, and its winter temperatures can drop far below freezing. In 1923, Roy Chapman Andrews found nests of fossil eggs at its Flaming Cliffs.
tossups.r: Hot examples of these places include the Sahara and the Kalahari. For 10 points, name these regions that get very little rain.

tossups.p: On hot days in these places, light bends as it passes through layers of air at different temperatures, creating mirages that look like pools of water on the ground. Because their dry air and clear skies let heat escape quickly, temperatures in these places can drop sharply after sunset.
tossups.r: Cacti, camels, and sand dunes are found in many of these places. For 10 points, name these very dry regions.

tossups.p: The Great Green Wall, an African Union project launched in 2007, aims to plant trees and restore land across the Sahel so that these places stop spreading. That spread of dry, barren land is often worsened by drought, overgrazing, and cutting down trees.
tossups.r: The largest hot one of these places, the Sahara, lies just north of the Sahel. For 10 points, name these regions that get very little rain.

trap.title: Not the Sahara
trap.body: Desert tossups often end with the Sahara, Antarctica, or the Atacama, and players who recognize one example blurt it out, but the question asks for the whole kind of place. Naming one desert, or a feature like “dunes” or “oasis,” is wrong. Remember that the largest desert is icy Antarctica; the Sahara is only the largest hot one.
trap.fix: Listen for “these places” or “these regions”: the answer is deserts. Rain shadows, cacti, camels, Köppen’s BW code, and less than about 25 centimeters of rain a year all point to deserts, not to any single example.
trap.line: Real answer line: Deserts (accept desert biome; do not accept “Sahara” or another single desert)
